title: I Love How Music Makes Soulframe Feel Like A Folktale
summary:
Soulframe still isn't out yet, but its Preludes were finally publicly opened on November 6, giving me my first chance to try it out. I was expecting "Warframe but fantasy," and to be fair, a lot of Soulframe is like that, but so much of Digital Extremes' new action-role-playing game feels very different. I'm floored--I've tried to get into Warframe several times and just kept bouncing off of it for one reason or another, but here I am really enjoying Soulframe and trying to figure out which live-service game I'm going to have to retire from to put Soulframe into my regular rotation. And it's really all because of the game's music.

Admittedly, music is one of the best parts about Warframe too. While I've never been able to really get into it, the reason I kept trying Warframe is because I'd keep hearing these absolute awesome sea shanties and vocal-led orchestral scores and thinking, "I want to play a game that sounds like that." But I never knew how to get to any of those moments to hear them play out in game. 

I tried getting into Warframe way too late, when the game had already transformed into something that largely catered to the players who were already in the ecosystem. The game just felt way too big of a beast to tackle as a newbie. Which is fine! That happens to every live-service game eventually.

Soulframe is new so it doesn't have that problem yet. And even if it did, it feels like it incorporates its music way more regularly and meaningfully than Warframe seems to. Almost every aspect of Soulframe (so far) is shaped around its music, including its poetry, birdsong, choral folktales, and orchestral scores. Character creation is writing a poem about how beautiful your mother was, several characters communicate solely in sing-song rhyme, and the first storyline revolves around learning the song that will not only play during the climatic boss battle but will also be played by your character in order to finally cleanse the evil you're fighting. 

In Soulframe, music is just implemented everywhere. It feels like a story that's meant to be listened to, like a folktale, and you just happen to be playing through it instead. The vibe is not dissimilar to games like South of Midnight or Kena: Bridge of Spirits.

I haven't experienced anything in terms of the gameplay that has wowed me thus far, but it's a solid baseline. It often feels like playing Dragon Age: Inquisition, so if you're like me and mourning the idea we'll never get another one of those, then Soulframe is surprisingly healing. 

At the start, you pick whether you want to strike enemies with a sword, be sneaky with daggers and a bow, or pepper foes with arcane pellets launched from your magical staff. Each of these roles has special abilities that work on a cooldown, and all classes can normally attack, defend, dodge, or jump. The semi-open world is broken up into several explorable sections populated with enemies that have a number above their head denoting whether you can take on a particular group or not, and as you complete side quests and main missions, you'll level up and be able to unlock new skills and equip better armor and weapons.

There's more to the gameplay, like combining certain abilities to take advantage of a staggered enemy or pulling out an enemy's soul to pull off a smite, but it's altogether a very simple loop--the kind you'd normally jump into with a podcast playing in the background so that you can unwind after a stressful day. And I suppose you could still do that here, but you're missing out by muting this game given how so much of the enjoyment comes from how characters talk and how the dynamism of the music causes moments of exploration and combat to flow together, again, like it's all one tale being conveyed. 

Plus, how else would you fully appreciate the pattern-focused rhythm minigames in which you have to play songs to charm animals, relive the memories of a place or person, travel between dimensions, and cleanse the corruption that's hurting a poor magical stag? Get outta here with your silly ocarina or tsuchibue. Soulframe's magical fipple flute is the superior gaming wind instrument!

Soulframe is already shaping up to have a pretty interesting story too. An enchanted melody (I'm telling you, music is everywhere in this game) known as the Spellsong has caused people to forget the importance of nature and the fey and the rites of true magick. But because you are born from an ancient fey lineage, you're able to resist the effects of the brainwashing. Blessed with the powerful song of the courageous Mora, spiritual Iridis, or graceful Saphene, you venture into a land in which humanity has put animals into cages, enslaved beasts with magical armor, and corrupted powerful spirits. 

You're basically a champion of nature, which isn't exactly a novel concept for a fantasy game, but I love how it's portrayed here. You fight humans to free captured animals and fey, destroy the armor of wardogs not to kill them but to free them, and challenge bosses to use the healing power of music to restore their memories of how the world is supposed to be: humanity and nature living side by side. Yeah, it's cheesy, but it feeds into that folktale vibe the rest of the game has going on.

There are certainly plenty of pretty games to look at this year, but Soulframe's Preludes might possess the most arresting sound of any game in 2026. I currently can't stop listening to it, even when I'm not playing the game. So if you're at all like me and have struggled to get into Warframe despite wanting to understand the hype, love a good folktale, or just have never cared about Grand Theft Auto and need something to play in November while everyone else is busy with GTA 6, consider downloading Soulframe. The Preludes are free-to-play, and while what's there is certainly not a full game, what's available feels like the bedrock for something that's going to be excellent.

title: “Physical” GTA 6 Copies Might Be Vulnerable To A Very Stupid But Serious Trick
summary:
Grand Theft Auto 6 ditched traditional discs for its "physical" launch, with Rockstar's game being sold as a digital code-in-box at retailers beginning this week. However, it appears a packaging choice may have accidentally left the game vulnerable to thieves--assuming they have a flashlight.

As shared on the forum ResetEra, users who received a physical version of Grand Theft Auto 6, at least in PEGI regions, report that the game's download code is printed directly on the inside of the cover rather than on a card or separate insert. When a flashlight is focused on the cover from the outside of the closed game case, the download code is visible in reverse.

In other words, there's a serious risk people could go into a store, do this trick, redeem the code, and leave the poor soul who actually buys the game off the shelf without GTA 6.

At this time, the trick does not seem to work on North American copies of GTA 6, as the code is intentionally obscured. Why Rockstar would not use this strategy on all regions is unclear. We've reached out to Rockstar for an explanation and will update this post if and when we receive a response.

If you happen to get your GTA 6 code stolen after paying $80, you can at least sleep soundly knowing that the thief can't play the game yet. Code-in-box copies, as well as digital preorders, all unlock for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S on November 19.

title: GTA 6 Owner Take-Two Is Not Interested In Selling Itself After EA Goes Private For $55 Billion
summary:
Recently, the gaming giant Electronic Arts was taken private in a $55 billion sale to an investor consortium led by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund. Could GTA 6 owner Take-Two be the next big company that gets acquired? Don't bet on it, CEO Strauss Zelnick says.

Speaking to David Rubenstein, Zelnick said Take-Two's business results have proven that it "can do very well as an independent company."

He said Take-Two's business is already "at scale" and healthy enough financially with a "terrific balance sheet," as he put it.

"We are not in a place where we need to be part of a bigger organization to be competitive. And in the entertainment business, scale matters," he said.

Zelnick said companies that do less than a billion in annual revenue might have issues with developing, marketing, and distributing games at scale. Not only that, but companies that don't generate a lot of money might not be able to survive the realities of the creative business, in which sometimes your product flops.

"But once you're over a billion dollars in annual revenue, and we're way beyond that point. Our guidance is $8 billion to $8.2 billion this fiscal year, additional scale doesn't seem to help you succeed."

In early 2008, Electronic Arts privately pursued a buyout of Take-Two, but after the GTA and BioShock company rejected it, EA went public in an attempt to get a deal done. Later that year, EA abandoned its plans to try to buy Take-Two after the GTA company said it was worth more and EA refused to increase its bid.

In 2019, it was rumored that Sony was attempting to buy Take-Two, but that was ultimately deemed to be unconfirmed market chatter and not a formal bid.

Take-Two has a market cap of more than $42 billion, and that is expected to grow in the year ahead, so it would seemingly take a lot of money to convince Take-Two to sell. Going forward, Zelnick has teased that new GTA games could release even faster, and that could be a positive for the company's financials.

GTA 6 launches on November 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. Preloading is underway now, and that's good news because the game has a massive file size.

title: GTA 6 Could Sell 55 Million Copies By Early Next Year, Report Says, And Average Selling Price Could Be $90
summary:
Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 launches on November 19, and it's expected to be a gigantic commercial success, but just how big will the launch be? Investor's Business Daily compiled data from a series of analyst reports about the game and its owner, Take-Two, and the consensus is that it's going to be a juggernaut.

In terms of sales, Brian Pitz of BMO Capital Markets said GTA 6 could sell 55 million copies during Take-Two's fiscal 2027, which ends on March 31, 2027. He said the game could sell 45 million units alone during the game's launch quarter, which is well ahead of the estimates of 34.2 million that IBD compiled.

 "This is an outlier in every respect," Circana's Mat Piscatella told the publication. "There have been some big game launches in the past, but nothing quite at this scale, not only in terms of the investment, but in terms of the anticipation. It's in its own league."

GTA 6 is launching with an $80 standard edition and a $100 Ultimate Edition. Raymond James analyst Andrew Marok said he's forecasting 50 million unit sales for the fiscal year 2027, and that the blended average selling price will be close to $90. According to Sensor Tower, early data suggested preorders were skewing toward the $100 edition, but by launch, it could be around 50/50.

Matthew Cost of Morgan Stanley, meanwhile, said if GTA 6 does indeed have strong sales out of the gate, this could create a "large potential audience" for the next iteration of GTA Online. Rockstar has not said anything yet about an online mode for GTA 6, but given the huge success of GTA Online for GTA 5, it's all but guaranteed that GTA 6 will incorporate online multiplayer as well.

Cost said this is a big deal for investors and may represent "the next major catalyst" for Take-Two's stock price. Take-Two's share price is down about 10% so far in 2026, and currently trades around $228/share..

A new version of GTA Online for GTA 6 would no doubt feature microtransactions and other ways to spend more money, and that could be frustrating for fans but great news for investors who want to see bigger returns.

D.A. Davidson analyst Wyatt Swanson said Take-Two's share price could surge to $300 in part because he believes Rockstar will release a PC edition of GTA 6 and usher in GTA Online 2.0. These releases would "enable structurally higher margins" for Take-Two, he said.

According to Sensor Tower, GTA 6 has already sold 12 million copies and generated $1.2 billion in revenue. GTA 5, meanwhile, took 72 hours to clear $1 billion in revenue--GTA 6 reached that a week before release, apparently.

GTA 6 launches on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S.

title: You Can Probably Guess WoW: Forever’s Most Popular Race, Class, And Faction
summary:
World of Warcraft: Forever has been in the wild for one week, and now we have all kinds of stats to sink our teeth into as they relate to the most popular races, classes, and faction in the latest version of developer Blizzard's MMORPG.

Forever launched November 4, becoming the biggest launch in WoW history by concurrent and returning players. Aside from that fact, Blizzard hasn't shared additional information on exactly how many characters have been made or what classes are most popular.

For that, we turn to Raider.IO, a WoW stat-tracking website more commonly used in the modern version of the game to provide rankings and details related to raids and Mythic+ progression. 

According to the site, close to 3.9 million characters have been created across all regions and rulesets so far. Around 48% of those characters are on the Alliance, with nearly 52% being on the Horde.

The most popular two races aren't all that surprising--undead and humans. Despite being the most boring choice imaginable, humans have always been a popular choice in WoW Classic thanks to their strong passives and the ability to be most classes. In Forever, they currently make up 37% of the Alliance population. Undead, on the other hand, are getting a massive boost from being the only Horde race to currently have access to Paladin. They make up nearly 40% of the Horde.

It won't shock you to learn then that Paladin is Forever's most-played class, with undead Paladin being the most-played race-and-class combo.

Skyborne elves are WoW's newest playable race, available to both factions. Around 10% of all characters are Skyborne, and faction-wise they are fairly even. Around 10% of Skyborne are Alliance and close to 11% are on the Horde. Consdiering how popular blood elves are in other versions of the game, the number of Skyborne feels low by comparison, though the fact they cost $30 to access probably has something to do with that.

As for what rulesets are most popular, the normal (PvE) server is far and away the biggest, with over 2 million characters. The PvP ruleset isn't too far behind with around 1.5 million characters. Those two rulesets dwarf the size of the game's two RP rulesets, which combined have around 250,000 players. 

With the exception of standard RP, every ruleset has a larger Horde population, a subject Blizzard recently commented on officially. In a forum post, Blizzard announced its goal is for PvP servers to be as close to 50/50 faction balance as possible, and would be placing restrictions on creating Horde characters on PvP rulesets in an effort to make that a reality.

"World of Warcraft: Forever's PvP is at its best when the Alliance and Horde are on equal footing, and we are dedicated to helping maintain that balance so that we can all witness battles at the epic scale that has made WoW: Forever PvP so memorable thus far," Blizzard said.  

One week after WoW: Forever's shockingly smooth launch, we've been impressed how visual updates and Blizzard's changes to the classic WoW formula have made the MMO feel brand new again. Forever received its first major class and dungeon changes earlier this week.

title: Magic: The Gathering Planeswalker Hits Netflix In 2027, Watch The Trailer Now
summary:
MagicCon: Atlanta has kicked off with The Preview Panel, which usually shows off cards from future sets. While Nauctis: The Sunken Realm did feature during the panel, Wizards of the Coast then gave the Atlanta crowd more information on Planeswalker, the upcoming animated series set in the Magic multiverse, which is coming to Netflix in 2027.

The two-minute teaser highlighted the animation team at Hungary-based Digic Pictures, along with showrunner Terry Matalas, Magic head of story Roy Graham, and more. A few brief moments of Chandra and Ajani were mixed in with the behind-the-scenes footage, offering a first look at the upcoming show's animation style.

Planeswalker's official description reveals that the show will follow Chandra, MTG's pyromancer planeswalker. She and other planeswalkers like Ajani must "harness their extraordinary abilities, navigate treacherous alliances, and battle their own inner demons to prevent a cataclysmic war that threatens to consume their very existence," according to the Netflix Tudum blog post.

A TV series for Magic: The Gathering is a long time coming, as the card game and its story have been going for over 30 years. title: Super Mario 3D Land Dared To Embrace 2D Mario In A 3D World
summary:
Super Mario 3D Land is celebrating its 15-year anniversary today, November 13, 2026. Below, we examine how 3D Land was a true iteration of the classic 2D Mario formula.

I remember when the first preview images of Super Mario 64 began circulating in gaming magazines. The thought of playing a Mario game in THREE DEEEEEE blew my tiny 8-year-old mind. While the final game was absolutely wonderful, it wasn’t quite what I had in my head when I thought about Mario gameplay translated into three dimensions. The worlds were vast and open-ended. Instead of running and jumping toward the goal, players had missions to accomplish. Puzzles to solve. Specific enemies to beat. Trinkets to find. Mario had a life bar. An air meter when underwater. Power-ups were temporary, vanishing after a certain time had elapsed.

And don’t get me wrong. It was different from what I imagined, but it worked. All of it worked. Nintendo had a winning formula on its hands, one that 3D Mario games would carry forward with Super Mario Sunshine and, to a lesser extent, the Super Mario Galaxy duology. But deep down, I couldn’t help but wonder what it would have been like in some alternate universe where they had adhered to the classic Mario formula instead in the move to 3D.

Thankfully, I didn’t have to wonder forever, because in 2011, Super Mario 3D Land released for the 3DS and changed what a 3D Mario game could be. How? By doing exactly what I wanted Super Mario 64 to do 15 years prior: fully translate the classic 2D Mario style and gameplay to the third dimension.

Even looking at 3D Land’s cover art evokes memories of the plumber’s colorful side-scrolling escapades. We see Mario hopping around a colorful environment full to the brim with blocks, pipes, platforms, even classic power-ups like the Fire Flower tucked away in the corner. And few elements could get the nostalgia juices flowing like the inclusion of the iconic Super Leaf from Super Mario Bros. 3. The game promised to be something different yet comfortingly familiar.

And what’s more comfortingly familiar than Bowser capturing Princess Peach and Mario racing off to rescue her? But even the simplest of Mario plots has to have at least one wrinkle. Due to a storm the night before, the land has been coated in Super Leaves, and now, Bowser and many of his minions have access to raccoon tails and the power of limited flight, just as Mario does.

Yes, the Super Leaf is the real star of the show here, marking the power-up’s first appearance in over two decades. You’d be hard-pressed to go through a level without either running into one of the raccoon power-ups or seeing one of Bowser’s minions imbued with it. Even the notoriously heavy Thwomps gracefully float about in the air as if they were light as feathers. 3D Land drills the point home that power-ups are back in a big way, no longer relegated to temporary usage as was the case with previous 3D titles. Joining the Tanooki Suit is the ever-classic Super Mushroom, allowing Mario to take an extra hit before dying—no life bar here!—and the aforementioned Fire Flower. New to the game is the Boomerang Suit, a spiritual successor to Super Mario Bros. 3’s Hammer Suit that can take out enemies coming and going (because it’s a boomerang, you see). Skilled players can go from level to level, even world to world, without ever losing the utility of a power-up at their disposal.

The power-ups wouldn’t be nearly as fun without great levels to use them in. 3D Land foregoes sprawling sandboxes for the more linear, self-contained, obstacle-course-like levels that first made Mario famous: Hop across colorful floating platforms, bonk some enemies, and slide down the flagpole at the end in classic Mario fashion. And at the end of each world, you take on Bowser (or at least a reasonable facsimile) on a bridge in a 3D variation of the classic boss fights from the original Super Mario Bros. This made 3D Land the perfect portable Mario game for bursts of quick fun on the go. It was 3D Mario in the palm of your hand when the Switch was still just a twinkle in Nintendo’s eye.

So, was this refreshing take on 3D Mario met with a warm reception from fans? Well, yeah, but not as much as I would have hoped.

Many fans decried 3D Land for deviating from the sandbox and exploratory gameplay the 3D games had showcased up to that point. To them, it felt “safe,” unwilling to take the big risks of its 3D predecessors.

To which I argue…what’s wrong with that? Despite being a smaller and more conservative Mario adventure, it did exactly what it sought out to do: make the  classic 2D Mario experience the foundation of a 3D Mario game for the first time. Even if it didn’t take any huge swings, the novelty of the concept is more than enough to make the game a classic in my eyes. And the fact that the game would pave the way for the fantastic Super Mario 3D World a few years later further demonstrates that the concept had legs. Super Mario 3D Land deserves to be judged on what it is, not what it isn’t. It was pure, distilled, classic 2D Mario on a three-dimensional plane, and I’ll remember it fondly for another 15 years.

title: After A Week With WoW: Forever, Classic WoW Feels New Again
summary:
It's been just over a week since the record-breaking launch of World of Warcraft: Forever. In that time a handful of players have raced to level 60, but the overwhelming majority are still weeks away from reaching max level, as they quest through Azeroth and see all the new sights and sounds Blizzard has cooked up.

So far, it's been (mostly) an absolute joy. I've spent every spare moment I can find in developer Blizzard's millennial retirement home, and after one week, it's safe to say I'm more than a little consumed by it. I was already a lover of original WoW, having grown up playing it, and have since spent thousands of hours playing WoW Classic after it launched in 2019. Having a new version of this MMORPG, one that's still unexplored and filled with new sights and sounds, is in many ways a dream come true.

That's not to say it's all sunshine and rainbows in Stormwind (or, if you prefer, Orgrimmar). Forever certainly has a lot going for it, and its launch was quite possibly the smoothest in Blizzard's entire history. That being said, while Forever is nearly everything I could want from a "Classic Plus" experience, I do have a few gripes I hope Blizzard takes a closer look at in the weeks and months to come. Here's what's working, what I'm most impressed by, and what I'm still on the fence about as we enter the second week of Forever.

Good - The World Is Alive

MMO launches are special occasions. It's when the game is likely to be the most populated it will ever be, and at any given moment you can see dozens of players running down the road, flooding questing areas, or hawking their wares in a capital city. 

Forever's launch was no exception, and it was, in a word, magical. Players were everywhere, and it made Azeroth feel alive again in a way that hasn't been seen since WoW Classic Season of Discovery. Massive crowds have been an issue in past WoW Classic launches, as everyone competes to tag enemies they need for quests or loot specific items, but I found it to be a relatively pain-free experience. This is mostly due to WoW: Forever's heavy use of layering, which divides players into different copies of the world. Layers were populated but not overcrowded, and it seems like after some initial tweaking, Blizzard has landed on what feels like the ideal number of players for various zones and cities.

It certainly helps that Blizzard's new lighting, fog, and weather tech does wonders to make Azeroth feel like a real place. Within the first hour of playing my dwarf Paladin, an intense snowstorm hit Dun Morogh. I knew about WoW: Forever's new weather effects, but I was floored at how immersive they can actually be. I could barely see 20 feet in front of me, relying on my map to tell me where to go. Already, within my first few hours of playing, I was being shown a version of Azeroth I'd never seen before. Later, while playing a Horde character in Orgrimmar, dark clouds formed overhead and heavy rain began to fall as I was turning in quests. The pitter-patter of heavy raindrops on the city's rocky pathways presented Orgrimmar in a whole new light.  It doesn't sound like much, but the game's updated visuals, particularly the weather effects, go a long way in making the world feel like a real place and not just a digital theme park. 

Good - New Content Feels Seamless

Much of what's exciting about Forever is its addition of all-new quests and dungeons to explore. From the get-go, Blizzard doesn't waste any time showing players what's changed, sprinkling in new quests and offering up a new low-level dungeon for both the Horde and Alliance.

New quests that let players select a gathering profession from the early starting zones are a godsend, letting you get a head start before venturing into the wider world. It's worth mentioning how little Forever's new quests stand out. To be clear, that's a good thing. They don't feel out of place, with similar "kill this many things" or "find this many items" objectives to vanilla WoW while still adding flavor to whatever zone or city they are found in. Sometimes their vague directions are reminiscent of classic WoW to the point of frustration, though you can always turn on the game's built-in quest tracking should you get too annoyed. 

Given how much time I've spent playing WoW Classic over the past six years, I'm usually keen on spotting when a quest is a new addition. It's a testament to the care Blizzard has put into these new quests that I sometimes have a hard time remembering whether a quest was always there or is actually a Forever exclusive. 

That goes for the new dungeons as well. The Ruins of Lordaeron and Hall of Thanes are too prominent, with too many quests associated with them for any OG WoW player to mistake them for part of the original game. Nonetheless, they fit right in. These are effective introductory dungeon experiences that build on existing lore and do a great job of showing what classic WoW's instanced content is all about--straightforward boss mechanics and the need to use your group's full toolkit to crowd control enemies and take out packs one at a time. It feels perfectly classic, and I can't wait to see what other new, higher-level dungeons have in store.

Good - The Joys Of Camping

Camping is one of a handful of new systems in Forever, and at first I was skeptical. Would players really take time they could be questing to sit around a campfire, get buffs, and work on professions? Given how efficiency-focused many in the WoW community are, I had my doubts.

Those doubts were quickly put to rest. Camping is a great addition to classic WoW that perfectly matches the game's pace, encouraging players to make connections, slow down, and smell the roses. In almost every questing hub I walked into, I found crowded campsites. Players shared the buffs available from their professions, crafted items, and made small talk as they waited to receive their experience buff after sitting by the camp for one minute. While I do worry that camping won't have much purpose at endgame, so far it's a welcome sight to see when out questing, serving as a beacon that brings players in an area together before they all go their separate ways.

Disappointing - Prohibitive Respec Costs

I hate to admit I may have messed up my talent tree in a moment of panic during a dungeon. No big deal, I thought. After all, I'm only level 14. I made my way to my nearest class trainer to reset my talent points, only to discover it costs an entire gold to respec. Guess I'm stuck living with my mistakes for the time being. 

Given how much each class's talent tree has changed in Forever, the high cost of respeccing and experimenting with different builds is a little disappointing, even if it is true to how the system worked in original WoW. As it is currently, I feel forced to continue down a certain path until my finances can afford the gold fee. That same feeling extends to the game's dual-specialization feature, which is locked until level 40 and costs 50 gold. It's great Forever has this as an option, but its steep cost and high level requirement mean few players will be taking advantage of it while leveling.

That's a shame, as it's already clear Forever, like every version of WoW before it, has a tank and healer shortage. Giving players a way to switch between healing, tank, or DPS specializations would encourage more experimentation and give hybrid-class players more options when it comes to grouping up. It's ultimately a problem that will likely fade away in a few months when most players have reached the endgame and gold is more plentiful, but for now, the gold costs associated with talents feel like a missed opportunity.

Off-Putting - Mount Collections And Store Items

I think every WoW Classic player knew this day would eventually come--Forever has an in-game store tab. Its inclusion seemed inevitable. Blizzard isn't going to put out a new version of WoW meant to last for decades without finding a new way to monetize it.

So far, there are only the various Skyborne packs available, but it's easy to imagine how in just a few months it could be flooded with various cosmetic appearances and mounts. That's all thanks to the addition of transmog and the new collections tab, which are features taken straight from the modern version of the game. I have to be honest: It's extremely offputting to open up the collections tab and see that, despite being only level one, I technically own two mounts from purchasing Forever's collector's edition. While I can't use them until level 40 and need the required (and expensive) riding training, it's still a bizarre sight to see.

It doesn't help that the new mounts and appearances look completely out of place. Unlike Forever's new quests and dungeons, which feel right at home, these premium cosmetics don't fit in with the rest of Forever's mostly classic-looking world. They are simply too detailed and high-res. The same can be said of the new Skyborne race, though Blizzard has already said it will be adding "standard definition" versions of them to the game early next year. I can only hope Blizzard will extend that level of care to everything it adds to the in-game shop in the future, because as of right now, these additions feel like they belong in the modern version of WoW, not Forever.

Wait And See - Legacy Talents Feel Underbaked

If there is one major new addition to Forever that I'm not quite sold on yet, it's the Legacy talent system. An account-wide achievement system of sorts, Legacy talents reward players with talent points for accomplishing various tasks. These talent points can then be spent in a passive perk tree, ranging from a small discount at vendors to longer food buffs, cheaper flight paths, increased reputation gains, and more.

To be perfectly honest, I haven't interacted much with this system as of yet, as you don't unlock it until level 25, when you earn your first Legacy talent point. But judging from the talents themselves and the requirements needed to gain them, I have some reservations. Most of the talents seem fairly inconsequential, while a handful seem too powerful and borderline mandatory.

The main fear I have is that those playing a single character won't unlock enough points to make the system feel useful. You get a single Legacy talent point for exploring the entirety of Azeroth (which is, frankly, absurd). You get three for achieving certain level milestones for each class, for a total of three at level 60. Those who level their first character to max can expect around 12 Legacy talent points in total, and that's if they level two professions up to max and complete every dungeon in the game at least once. At launch, players can only spend a total of 16 Legacy points per character, though they can earn more.

That's a lot of work for not much payoff. I get that the goal is to give players a reason to make new characters and work toward some form of account-wide progression, but currently, the system feels more like a nice bonus that you get for just playing the game than a reward for accomplishing specific goals or feats. I'm sure Blizzard will continue to flesh the system out and refine it, but for something that was billed as a game-changing feature exclusive to Forever, it mostly seems like it could be removed entirely and I wouldn't even notice. 

No doubt I'll have more to say about Forever as I continue making progress towards the endgame. There's a huge amount to see, do, and uncover, and even after an entire week, I've only just scratched the surface. I still have dozens of levels to gain, dungeons to conquer, and new zones to explore. It's the journey, not the destination, that counts, and I have a long journey ahead. Best not to keep Azeroth waiting.

Wait And See - Legacy Talents Feel Underbaked

If there is one major new addition to Forever that I'm not quite sold on yet, it's the Legacy talent system. An account-wide achievement system of sorts, Legacy talents reward players with talent points for accomplishing various tasks. These talent points can then be spent in a passive perk tree, ranging from a small discount at vendors to longer food buffs, cheaper flight paths, increased reputation gains, and more.

To be perfectly honest, I haven't interacted much with this system as of yet, as you don't unlock it until level 25, when you earn your first Legacy talent point. But judging from the talents themselves and the requirements needed to gain them, I have some reservations. Most of the talents seem fairly inconsequential, while a handful seem too powerful and borderline mandatory.

The main fear I have is that those playing a single character won't unlock enough points to make the system feel useful. You get a single Legacy talent point for exploring the entirety of Azeroth (which is, frankly, absurd). You get three for achieving certain level milestones for each class, for a total of three at level 60. Those who level their first character to max can expect around 12 Legacy talent points in total, and that's if they level two professions up to max and complete every dungeon in the game at least once. At launch, players can only spend a total of 16 Legacy points per character, though they can earn more.

That's a lot of work for not much payoff. I get that the goal is to give players a reason to make new characters and work toward some form of account-wide progression, but currently, the system feels more like a nice bonus that you get for just playing the game than a reward for accomplishing specific goals or feats. I'm sure Blizzard will continue to flesh the system out and refine it, but for something that was billed as a game-changing feature exclusive to Forever, it mostly seems like it could be removed entirely and I wouldn't even notice. 

No doubt I'll have more to say about Forever as I continue making progress towards the endgame. There's a huge amount to see, do, and uncover, and even after an entire week, I've only just scratched the surface. I still have dozens of levels to gain, dungeons to conquer, and new zones to explore. It's the journey, not the destination, that counts, and I have a long journey ahead. Best not to keep Azeroth waiting.

title: The Best Video Game Soundtracks Of 2026 (So Far)
summary:
Video games don't just look better than ever, thanks to imaginative art directions and cutting-edge graphics; they also sound fantastic. With some of the best talent in the industry composing new soundtracks, it's sadly too easy for some of these superb albums to fly under your radar.

To keep track of the best that 2026 has to offer, we're collecting the best video game soundtracks available and listing them below alongside official channels like Spotify, YouTube, and Tidal so that you can listen to them yourself. And if those games also have a snazzy vinyl that you can add to your collection? You can bet your axe we'll also include a link for that modern-day art.

We'll update this list regularly throughout the year, so check back often to see what's been added. While you're here, you might also want to check out our list for the best games of 2026.

Cairn

By Martin Stig Andersen, The Toxic Avenger, and Gildaa

Why should you climb a mountain? Because it's there. Why should you listen to the Cairn soundtrack? Same reason, but also because it perfectly complements the game, giving the entire experience an awe-inspiring feel as you grasp for an out-of-reach handhold. Just like Cairn, the soundtrack is calm, meditative, and full of audio elements that add a cosmic flair to this mountaineering adventure.

Where to listen:

  • YouTube
  • Spotify
  • Apple Music

Esoteric Ebb

By Anders Bach, Kristian Paulsen, and Brian Batz

Usually, a video game soundtrack has a common theme that carries through each of its tracks, uniting them into a single album. The score for Esoteric Ebb is an exception to that rule, as it effortlessly shifts between genres and motifs, constantly surprising and delighting your senses with its eclectic mix. One song might evoke images of a faraway land during Arthurian times, and another track might sound perfect for a 16-bit beat-'em-up, making this album a treasure trove of audio treats that reflect the game's tabletop inspirations. If you're interested in the game and the soundtrack, Steam offers both as a bundle deal.

Where to listen:

  • YouTube
  • Spotify
  • Bandcamp

Marathon

By Ryan Lott

Marathon's soundtrack e is a magical sample of electronic music that captures the sense of mystery at the heart of the game. There's an ethereal quality to these tunes, and with a distinctive arrangement that's already spurring several mesmerizing remixes within the growing Marathon community, we're hoping the rest of the score is as bold and energetic as what we've been treated to so far. It's a blend of propulsive rhythms, electronic textures, and experimental sound design that makes for an unforgettable score.

Where to listen:

  • YouTube
  • Spotify (Vol 1)
  • Spotify (Vol 2)
  • Apple Music (Vol 1)
  • Apple Music (Vol 2)

Mewgenics

By Ridiculon

You'd expect a soundtrack for a video game about genetically engineered cats being sent to do battle against strange enemies to be suitably weird, and Ridiculon doesn't disappoint on this front. The Mewgenics score combines a punchy, folksy sound with the inner workings of a cat's mind, and as you'd guess, those finger-snappin' thoughts typically translate to milk and murder. An ode to the absurdity of Mewgenics, Ridiculon's Matthias Bossi and Jon Evans have crafted a surreal soundtrack to enjoy for one of 2026's best games.

Where to listen:

  • YouTube
  • Spotify
  • Apple Music

Mixtape

By various artists

Every game on this list (so far) has made it on the strength of its original soundtrack. Mixtape is the exception with its selection of licensed tracks, not because they're expertly curated, but because they're the exact kind of needle-drops that remind you why music is such a powerful force in our lives. It's the raw emotion of these songs juxtaposed against the coming-of-age story that works so well, effortlessly blending a heartfelt story with the kind of music that makes you want to pump your fist in the air. From Joy Division to Silverchair, Mixtape's choice of music is a greatest hits album dedicated to teenage rebellion and freedom, expertly paired with a touching coming-of-age story.

Where to listen:

  • YouTube

People of Note

By Big Giant Circles

When we look back at 2026, it's going to be clear just how good the year was for fans of rhythmic video games. People of Note is a great example, as it brings that stadium energy to your screen that only a handful of megastars are capable of generating. It's the grandest of music, energetic beats designed to get your blood pumping and your body moving in a turn-based RPG format. The visuals and audio are top-notch, pairing together like a fine wine and cheese combo for your ears.

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • Bandcamp
  • YouTube Music
  • Apple Music

Scott Pilgrim EX

By Anamanaguchi

A new Anamanaguchi soundtrack is always cause for celebration, but when the band is putting its considerable talents toward a Scott Pilgrim project? That's a reason to bring the house down. The band returns to Toronto for a whopping 71-song soundtrack, and as you'd expect, the score is a fist-pumping collection of punchy tracks that fuses nostalgic sounds with enough energy to knock the highlights out of your hair.

Where to listen:

  • YouTube
  • Spotify
  • Apple Music

Where to buy:

  • Polyvinyl Store

Screamer

By Max Aruj

When it comes to racing games, soundtracks for this genre need to feel like a jolt of nitrous oxide being delivered straight to your ears. Screamer doesn't disappoint, as the anime-inspired cyberpunk racing game has you cruising through the streets at an irresponsible speed while your head bops along to the high-energy score. Each track motivates you to push your revs into the red, motivating you to go faster and tear around corners with reckless abandon in a race where the only rule that matters is the Rule of Cool.

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

Denshattack

By Tee Lopes, Sean Bialo, and Andrew One, featuring various artists

Not just one of the best games of 2026, Denshattack offers pure bangers for your buck thanks to a score featuring 80 tracks. Featuring a star-studded lineup of artists--led by main composers Tee Lopes, Sean Bialo, and Andrew One--the music perfectly complements the energetic gameplay while also channeling the sound of beloved turn-of-the-millennium Dreamcast classics like Jet Set Radio and Sonic Adventure. There's a lot to love about this soundtrack, and with over four hours of music, you'll be tapping your feet to breakbeat, funk, acid jazz, hip-hop, punk, and J-pop tracks for a long time.

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • YouTube
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal
  • Bandcamp

Mina the Hollower

By Jake Kaufman

There's a charm to classical 8-bit music, and Mina the Hollower captures that audio magic with surprisingly complex chiptunes to dig into. An old adage among artists says limitations can lead to creativity, and composer Jake Kaufman certainly knows how to squeeze an incredible amount of depth from a retro collection of sounds and tools to build an impressively massive soundtrack. With Streets of Rage composer Yuzo Koshiro also lending his talents to this 96-track, four-hour score, Mina the Hollower sounds delightfully inviting and unsettling.

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • YouTube
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

007 First Light

By Alexis Smith and Joe Henson of The Flight

The soundtrack for 007 First Light works so well because composers Alexis Smith and Joe Henson of The Flight deliberately held back on dropping the classical Bond theme too early in the game. Instead, you're tasked with earning that signature theme, and the duo builds up to that moment with an orchestral arrangement that seamlessly transitions between moments of stealth, brawls, and car chases. Fusing it with hybrid electronic arrangements gave the game an audio atmosphere rivaling a big-budget Hollywood movie, and once you finally hear those familiar notes in all their brass glory, you can't help but roll credits on 007 First Light with a massive smile on your face.

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • YouTube
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

Scritchy Scratchy

By Clothing Club

Many of the soundtracks on this list feature high-energy arrangements, but Clothing Club's score for Scritchy Scratchy is just cool as a cucumber. With retro beats and a terrific groove, these tracks are designed as background music that doesn't distract from the super-satisfying scratch-card incremental game, but it's also great for those days when you need some lo-fi vibes in your life.

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • YouTube
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

Lumentale: Memories of Trey

By Tiziano Bellu, Giovanni Santolla, and Lorenzo Varriano

Lumentale: Memories of Trey is a fun spin on the monster-collecting formula, but at its heart is a surprisingly delicate soundtrack. A powerhouse of Italian composers has put together something that's not only special, but also downright massive, as the score spans three distinct volumes: Mythos, Logos, and Battle+Extra. The end result? A beautifully retro orchestral arrangement that is nostalgic and atmospheric. Nier fans are in for a treat, too, as acclaimed singer Emi Evans lends her vocals to the end credits of this delightful game.

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • YouTube
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls

By Toma Otowa

Arc System Works knows not only how to make a great fighting game, but how to pair it with a fantastic soundtrack to complement a few rounds of digital fisticuffs. The soundtrack for Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls doesn't disappoint, combining incredible audio variety and surprising collaborations to create dozens of character and stage themes. With EDM, heavy metal, and orchestral music featured prominently, headlined by the "Stronger as One" main theme, you get a buffet of high-energy music to enjoy while you fight to save the world from Avengers-level threats.

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

The Adventures of Elliot: The Millennium Tales

By Tomohiro Nakamachi and Yuto Moritani

Unsurprisingly, the music of The Adventures of Elliot: The Millennium Tales is a nostalgic throwback to the golden age of JRPGs. The best tracks on this mammoth 105-song collection have warmth and depth, and each one blends into the background, selling you on the idea that you're taking part in a magical, whimsical journey across faraway fantasy lands.

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • Apple Music

MIO Memories in Orbit

By Nicolas Guéguen

Juxtaposition is the main takeaway of the MIO: Memories in Orbit soundtrack, as the music beautifully blends traditional sounds with mechanical melodies. Across 75 tracks, you can feel the isolation and scale of "The Vessel" where the game takes place, with the dynamic pacing mirroring the experience of tight soulslike combat and melancholic exploration. There's a blurred line between sentient beings and programmed machines in MIO Memories in Orbit, and Nicolas Guéguen's score captures those sci-fi themes and pumps them right back into your ears.

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • YouTube
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

Bubsy 4D

By Fat Bard

I don't know if I can trust reality anymore, because 2026 being the year of Bubsy was not on my bingo card. Not only is Bubsy 4D a surprisingly good adventure game that doesn't make me want to yeet my TV out the nearest window, but indie video game audio duo Fat Bard have managed to craft a score that I genuinely enjoy listening to during the day. It has '90s Saturday morning cartoon energy and dynamic instrumentation, and it's incredibly catchy. This should come as no surprise given the composers' pedigree, as this upbeat soundtrack is an eclectic treat.

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • YouTube
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

Saros

By Sam Slater

How do you sum up the sound of Saros in three words or less? Pure, atmospheric dread. Composer Sam Slater nails the idea of playing a game in which an eclipse brings terrifying changes to the world around you. That creeping sense of tension from the soundtrack is embedded deep within every pixel-pore of Saros, with the music warping and distorting to reflect the planetary changes around you as you descend deeper into a dangerous labyrinth. It's a heavy score, frequently punctuated by raw guitar riffs and unconventional instruments that add an otherworldly layer to Saros.

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • YouTube
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

Phonopolis

By Tomáš Dvořák

Phonopolis's avant-garde quality is reflected in its score, as composer Tomáš Dvořák clearly wasn't afraid to try experimental ideas. Every song has a raw, lo-fi theme that sounds intentional, heavily processed, and loud, music that could only work in a handcrafted game centered on loudspeakers and an authoritarian leader controlling a city through audio propaganda. Every track introduces something new, and each one feels like an entire album has been crammed into it. That sheer density of ideas makes the Phonopolis soundtrack a standout collection of music in a year full of incredible albums.

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • YouTube
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced

By Brian Tyler and featuring new tracks by Stephen Lukach

What's old is new again, and in the case of Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced, I don't think anyone will complain about getting a selection of familiar, new, and improved sea shanties to sing along to. Bryan Tyler's score sounds better than ever, thanks to Ubisoft taking a technical pass of the original soundtrack. Dynamic remixing and rebalanced audio make those authentic sailor songs punctuate a battle on the high seas. All that, and several brand-new orchestral pieces specifically tailored for key emotional story beats, made this an album worth returning to.

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • YouTube
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

Silent Hill: Townfall

By Anthony Scott Burns

Composer Anthony Scott Burns nailed the assignment for Silent Hill: Townfall, as this score effectively captured the atmospheric dread of the Konami psychological-horror series. At the same time, it introduces its own audio identity to the franchise, mixing melancholic piano lines and decaying synth textures to create a brooding ambient soundscape that helps build tension. It's a score that feels intimately tied to the fog-drenched streets of St. Amelia and enhanced by analog decay to sell you on the game's theme of fragmented memories. 

Resident Evil movie soundtrack

By Hays Holladay and Ryan Holladay

Can a movie soundtrack deliver a jump-scare? It certainly feels like it with Zach Cregger's Resident Evil film, and yes, we're cheating slightly on this list—it's video game-adjacent, so it makes the cut. Composed by Hays and Ryan Holladay, the soundtrack is a masterclass in tension, using pulsing sounds and haunting vocal threads to deliver retro-modern synth-horror audio. Mirroring the movie's creeping dread, it complements the visceral scenes and, on its own, is an eerie composition that underscores the film's tragic, inescapable doom.

Where to listen:

  • YouTube
  • Spotify
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

Street Fighter movie soundtrack

By Leo Birenberg and Zach Robinson

The Street Fighter might be a box office bomb, but on my rotating playlist, it's an absolute winner. Like the underrated movie, every note in this score feels like a reference to the video game source material, mixing revamped character themes with original tunes. Negative Edge is worth the price of admission alone, but once you start cycling in other tracks, you're in for several rounds of audio knockouts.

Where to listen:

  • YouTube
  • Spotify
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

Big Walk

By aksfx (Ben Esposito and Michael Cole)

There's a lot to love about Big Walk, but its soundtrack is a standout feature. It's playful, joyful music that perfectly captures the atmosphere of exploration and discovery that makes the game so great, elevating the experience whenever you hear it. That's the secret sauce of this score, because it pops into play only when you actually need to hear it, instead of being a constant presence. That approach makes each track hit hard at the right time, making each song from this eclectic mix feel like a little audio reward for solving one of the game's many puzzles. Who would have thought that a soundtrack about wayward ducks could hit this hard? Not us, that's for sure!

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • YouTube
  • Bandcamp

Control Resonant

The audio design of Control Resonant is one of our favorite things about the game--along with its stunning art direction--and Petri Alanko's score only adds to its charm. Spanning a baker's dozen of moody, brutalist tunes, this soundtrack complements the game's style and tone perfectly. Whether you're experiencing atmospheric liminal terror or working your way through a version of Manhattan where the rules of reality don't always apply, that music and how it's executed make for an experienced dance partner as you weave through mobs of Hiss and otherworldly foes in your quest to save the day. Also worth mentioning is Zoe's mixtape, a curated selection of hard-rocking tracks that add extra percussive spice to Remedy's wonderfully strange game.

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • YouTube
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

Unsurprisingly, the music of The Adventures of Elliot: The Millennium Tales is a nostalgic throwback to the golden age of JRPGs. The best tracks on this mammoth 105-song collection have warmth and depth, and each one blends into the background, selling you on the idea that you're taking part in a magical, whimsical journey across faraway fantasy lands.

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • Apple Music

MIO Memories in Orbit

By Nicolas Guéguen

Juxtaposition is the main takeaway of the MIO: Memories in Orbit soundtrack, as the music beautifully blends traditional sounds with mechanical melodies. Across 75 tracks, you can feel the isolation and scale of "The Vessel" where the game takes place, with the dynamic pacing mirroring the experience of tight soulslike combat and melancholic exploration. There's a blurred line between sentient beings and programmed machines in MIO Memories in Orbit, and Nicolas Guéguen's score captures those sci-fi themes and pumps them right back into your ears.

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • YouTube
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

Bubsy 4D

By Fat Bard

I don't know if I can trust reality anymore, because 2026 being the year of Bubsy was not on my bingo card. Not only is Bubsy 4D a surprisingly good adventure game that doesn't make me want to yeet my TV out the nearest window, but indie video game audio duo Fat Bard have managed to craft a score that I genuinely enjoy listening to during the day. It has '90s Saturday morning cartoon energy and dynamic instrumentation, and it's incredibly catchy. This should come as no surprise given the composers' pedigree, as this upbeat soundtrack is an eclectic treat.

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • YouTube
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

Saros

By Sam Slater

How do you sum up the sound of Saros in three words or less? Pure, atmospheric dread. Composer Sam Slater nails the idea of playing a game in which an eclipse brings terrifying changes to the world around you. That creeping sense of tension from the soundtrack is embedded deep within every pixel-pore of Saros, with the music warping and distorting to reflect the planetary changes around you as you descend deeper into a dangerous labyrinth. It's a heavy score, frequently punctuated by raw guitar riffs and unconventional instruments that add an otherworldly layer to Saros.

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • YouTube
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

Phonopolis

By Tomáš Dvořák

Phonopolis's avant-garde quality is reflected in its score, as composer Tomáš Dvořák clearly wasn't afraid to try experimental ideas. Every song has a raw, lo-fi theme that sounds intentional, heavily processed, and loud, music that could only work in a handcrafted game centered on loudspeakers and an authoritarian leader controlling a city through audio propaganda. Every track introduces something new, and each one feels like an entire album has been crammed into it. That sheer density of ideas makes the Phonopolis soundtrack a standout collection of music in a year full of incredible albums.

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • YouTube
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced

By Brian Tyler and featuring new tracks by Stephen Lukach

What's old is new again, and in the case of Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced, I don't think anyone will complain about getting a selection of familiar, new, and improved sea shanties to sing along to. Bryan Tyler's score sounds better than ever, thanks to Ubisoft taking a technical pass of the original soundtrack. Dynamic remixing and rebalanced audio make those authentic sailor songs punctuate a battle on the high seas. All that, and several brand-new orchestral pieces specifically tailored for key emotional story beats, made this an album worth returning to.

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • YouTube
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

Silent Hill: Townfall

By Anthony Scott Burns

Composer Anthony Scott Burns nailed the assignment for Silent Hill: Townfall, as this score effectively captured the atmospheric dread of the Konami psychological-horror series. At the same time, it introduces its own audio identity to the franchise, mixing melancholic piano lines and decaying synth textures to create a brooding ambient soundscape that helps build tension. It's a score that feels intimately tied to the fog-drenched streets of St. Amelia and enhanced by analog decay to sell you on the game's theme of fragmented memories. 

Resident Evil movie soundtrack

By Hays Holladay and Ryan Holladay

Can a movie soundtrack deliver a jump-scare? It certainly feels like it with Zach Cregger's Resident Evil film, and yes, we're cheating slightly on this list—it's video game-adjacent, so it makes the cut. Composed by Hays and Ryan Holladay, the soundtrack is a masterclass in tension, using pulsing sounds and haunting vocal threads to deliver retro-modern synth-horror audio. Mirroring the movie's creeping dread, it complements the visceral scenes and, on its own, is an eerie composition that underscores the film's tragic, inescapable doom.

Where to listen:

  • YouTube
  • Spotify
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

Street Fighter movie soundtrack

By Leo Birenberg and Zach Robinson

The Street Fighter might be a box office bomb, but on my rotating playlist, it's an absolute winner. Like the underrated movie, every note in this score feels like a reference to the video game source material, mixing revamped character themes with original tunes. Negative Edge is worth the price of admission alone, but once you start cycling in other tracks, you're in for several rounds of audio knockouts.

Where to listen:

  • YouTube
  • Spotify
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

Big Walk

By aksfx (Ben Esposito and Michael Cole)

There's a lot to love about Big Walk, but its soundtrack is a standout feature. It's playful, joyful music that perfectly captures the atmosphere of exploration and discovery that makes the game so great, elevating the experience whenever you hear it. That's the secret sauce of this score, because it pops into play only when you actually need to hear it, instead of being a constant presence. That approach makes each track hit hard at the right time, making each song from this eclectic mix feel like a little audio reward for solving one of the game's many puzzles. Who would have thought that a soundtrack about wayward ducks could hit this hard? Not us, that's for sure!

Where to listen:

  • Spotify
  • YouTube
  • Bandcamp

Control Resonant

The audio design of Control Resonant is one of our favorite things about the game--along with its stunning art direction--and Petri Alanko's score only adds to its charm. Spanning a baker's dozen of moody, brutalist tunes, this soundtrack complements the game's style and tone perfectly. Whether you're experiencing atmospheric liminal terror or working your way through a version of Manhattan where the rules of reality don't always apply, that music and how it's executed make for an experienced dance partner as you weave through mobs of Hiss and otherworldly foes in your quest to save the day. Also worth mentioning is Zoe's mixtape, a curated selection of hard-rocking tracks that add extra percussive spice to Remedy's wonderfully strange game.

  • YouTube
  • Apple Music
  • Tidal

title: Official Zelda Website Raises Eyebrows By Labeling 3DS Game As Playable On Switch
summary:
Nintendo is celebrating The Legend of Zelda's 40th anniversary in many different ways, but one detail on the company's official website raised confusion--and curiosity-- about a classic 3DS Zelda game.

A "History" page on Nintendo's website lists every mainline Zelda game in release order, including the release date and which platforms you can play for each entry. The site marks every game that's playable for Nintendo Switch Online subscribers--and the 2013 3DS game The Legend of Zelda: A Link Between Worlds was marked as such. The NSO icon has since been removed from the site.

Currently, the Nintendo Classics library allows NSO subscribers to play select NES, SNES, and Game Boy games, while the Expansion Pack subscription includes access to Nintendo 64, Game Boy Advance, GameCube, and Virtual Boy games. There's currently no way to play 3DS games on Nintendo Switch, prompting the question of whether this was an error on Nintendo's website or an accidental leak that A Link Between Worlds will somehow be playable on Switch. GameSpot has reached out to Nintendo for clarification on the matter.

The site appropriately labels the Zelda games featured on Nintendo Classics if they are only playable with the Nintendo Switch Online Expansion Pack subscription, which applies to Ocarina of Time (the original), Majora's Mask, A Link to the Past/Four Swords on GBA, The Wind Waker, and The Minish Cap.

If this labeling for A Link Between Worlds were true, it would be surprising if the Expansion Pack were not required to play it. Nintendo Classics also lacks any Wii or DS games, so jumping straight to 3DS would be a bizarre move for the service.

Whatever the case, A Link Between Worlds is a magnificent entry in the Zelda series that deserves to be experienced. GameSpot's 9/10 review of the game called it an "absolute treat to play" with some of the "best Zelda dungeons in years."

title: GTA 6 And These Other Games Can Justify An $80 Price, Expert Says
summary:
Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 finally releases on November 19, and you'll have to pay at least $80 for it. That's a full $20 more than what GTA 5 cost in 2013 and $10 more than many other big AAA games today. Is $80 going to become the "new normal" for AAA games, or is it, along with Nintendo's Mario Kart World and Tears of the Kingdom for Switch 2, an outlier at $80?

According to Alinea Analytics researcher Rhys Elliott, $80 won't be an across-the-board new price for all games. Some developers will purposefully price their games lower to draw in more consumers--he pointed to games like Expedition 33 ($50), Phantom Blade Zero ($60), and Oblivion Remastered ($50) as examples.

Elliott said that when GTA 6 inevitably becomes a huge success with its $80 and $100 editions, some publishers will be "jumping for joy" because they'll take this as a signal that the market will indeed accept these higher prices.

However, Elliott said he hopes the industry doesn't learn the wrong lessons from GTA 6 and its $80 price point. "GTA 6 is as inelastic as things get in entertainment. People will pay anything to get their mitts on this one, which makes it seem like the perfect Trojan horse for an industry-wide price rise," he said.

"The $80 price point will be a Godsend to some publishers, but it’ll be a snowball's chance in hell for others. After all, this kind of stuff can be zero-sum. When a player spends $100 on GTA 6, their remaining budget shrinks," he added.

Elliott went on to list off some of the studios and game franchises that could likely get their fanbases to buy in at $80. He said these include the next big God of War game after Laufey, the next Naughty Dog game, Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet, and future Forza titles (assuming Xbox strips them out of Game Pass). Additionally, Elliott said From Software "has the cache" to charge $80 for its new games, while Hogwarts Legacy 2 could also up the price to $80. Elliott added that some of the top sports games could charge more, but that might be a tougher sell considering those games are full of microtransactions already.

"So not all games were created equal, and mid-tier AAA publishers--and also bigger publishers offering smaller games or remakes--will price downward at $40-$60," Elliott said.

There are a lot of factors at play here. For starters, GTA 5 launched at $60 back in 2013, and that same $60 is worth $86 today after inflation, making GTA 6--at least its $80 edition--effectively cheaper than GTA 5.

At the same time, many people are acutely aware that their pay has not kept up with inflation, while the federal minimum wage hasn't moved up since 2009. GTA 6 is also coming out at a rough time for many people, with gas and grocery prices surging, and the cost of everyday goods generally spiking due in part to increasing inflation. And anyone heading to a store to buy a console to play GTA 6 on is in for some serious sticker shock, as game consoles today are more expensive than ever due to the AI craze.

New video games generally staying the same price over the years has had serious negative effects on the entire industry, experts have said. It's part of the reason why publishers now try to squeeze people more with DLC, battle passes, microtransactions, collector's editions, paid early access, and more. Recently, an Xbox advertising chief said price increases would be a hard sell, so the company is turning to ads to help offset ballooning budgets and keep the business healthy.

title: Friday The 13th Is Finally Returning To Movies, But Are Games Next?
summary:
Everyone's favorite hockey-mask-wearing killer is finally set to return to the big screen for the first time in almost two decades, with a new film starring him set for release in 2027.

Per Deadline, veteran Friday the 13th director Steve Miner--who directed Friday the 13th: Part 2, Part 3, and the Halloween H20: 20 Years Later film that featured Jason's mask-wearing rival, Michael Myers--will helm this project. The Friday the 13th franchise has been largely absent from cinema, as a grueling battle over the franchise rights played out for years between screenwriter Victor Miller and production companies Horror, Inc. and the Manny Company (backed by original producer Sean S. Cunningham).

Fast-forward to 2026, and things have been settled. Miller has ownership of elements introduced in his original Friday the 13th screenplay--including Camp Crystal Lake, Pamela Voorhees, and the child version of Jason--while Cunningham's company retains foreign distribution rights to the original film, ownership of all sequels, and the trademark on the adult version of Jason Voorhees, who was introduced in later installments.

Because neither side can use the full Friday the 13th mythology alone, both camps came together with the film studio A24, which acts as a neutral bridge between them. Both sides receive executive producer credits on Jason projects, and this also saw the launch of the Jason Universe to foster broader franchise cooperation. Thanks to that new sense of collaboration, we got the Friday the 13th prequel series Crystal Lake, which has proven to be something of a critical hit.

For film fans, this will be the first Jason movie since the 2009 reboot, which arrived as Hollywood's obsession with remaking horror movies was winding down. While that was the last we'd see of Jason and his machete on the silver screen for many years, the character lived on in the fun video game adaptation first released in 2017. Sadly, the game was delisted on December 31, 2023, after developer Gun Media's IP rights to Friday the 13th expired, but its popularity helped spark a new wave of multiplayer games based on popular horror franchises like Evil Dead and The Texas Chain Saw Massacre.

Jason would appear in Fortnite and Call of Duty, and following the announcement of the Jason Universe, Horror Inc. executive vice president Robbie Barsamian teased plans for a new Friday the 13th video game. Meanwhile, 2026 has been headlined by two great games based on classic horror movie IPs. In September, players took on the role of the Shape in Halloween: The Game, and in October, Hellraiser: Revival resurrected Pinhead for a pretty extreme adventure.

event_model_payload.summary:
2026 has entered the home stretch, and it has been a very exciting year for video games. In addition to being the first full year for the Switch 2, 2026 will also see the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, which is widely anticipated as one of the biggest entertainment launches of all time. We'll see plenty of other sequels to popular franchises, as well as a number of brand-new games across everything from console to mobile.

In order for you to keep track of everything coming in 2026, GameSpot has broken down the entire year by month, showing games with final release dates as well as games given a nebulous "2026" window. As more games are announced, they'll be added to this list, and those given final dates will be shifted into the relevant sections. For more, check out all the games released in 2025.
